title: A quote that loses a cent
summary: Fix integer monetary calculations and validate an invoice quote without changing its API.

stages.title: Understand the contract
stages.brief: Fix integer monetary calculations and validate an invoice quote without changing its API. Preserve the documented public interface. Use only Python 3.11 standard-library modules.
requirements: Keep quote_total(lines, discount_bps=0, shipping_cents=0) and return an integer number of cents.
Each LineItem has an integer unit_cents >= 0 and integer quantity >= 1; booleans, floats, and strings are invalid.
discount_bps must be an integer from 0 through 10000; shipping_cents must be an integer >= 0. Booleans are invalid.
Compute the subtotal, apply the discount once at invoice level, round half up to cents, then add undiscounted shipping. Avoid floating-point arithmetic.
Empty inputs are valid and return shipping; accept a one-pass iterable without mutating its items. Raise ValueError for invalid values.

stages.title: Implement the change
stages.brief: Make the smallest coherent change that satisfies the disclosed contract.
requirements: Preserve public interfaces and existing valid behavior.

stages.title: Verify the behavior
stages.brief: Run checks and inspect failures before finishing.
requirements: Run public checks and add a targeted boundary or regression check.
Identify behavior that your tests do not establish.

stages.title: Defend your decisions
stages.brief: Explain the submitted code and its remaining limits.
requirements: Use concrete code or test evidence.
Describe one alternative and its trade-off.

rubric.name: Exact monetary behavior
rubric.description: Use the stated integer and rounding contract.

anchors.strong: Uses integer arithmetic and rounds the invoice subtotal once, including half-cent boundaries and large amounts.
anchors.developing: Normal totals work, but rounding or large-value behavior has gaps.
anchors.needsWork: Uses float arithmetic or an incorrect rounding level and cannot explain the resulting cent error.

rubric.name: Validation boundaries
rubric.description: Reject invalid values before computing a quote.

anchors.strong: Checks exact integer types, bounds, and all iterable items; raises the documented error.
anchors.developing: Validates common negative values but misses booleans or parameter boundaries.
anchors.needsWork: Accepts invalid amounts/quantities or returns misleading totals.

rubric.name: Verification and reasoning
rubric.description: Support behavior with focused checks and explain limits.

anchors.strong: Tests boundary cases and explains why ordinary totals alone cannot catch rounding errors.
anchors.developing: Runs happy-path checks but leaves a known boundary unverified.
anchors.needsWork: Treats a successful ordinary example as proof of all monetary behavior.

probes.question: Which input makes the old quote lose a cent, and what does your implementation do differently?
How do you distinguish a valid integer amount from True in Python?
What would change if the discount had to be rounded for each line rather than for the invoice?

hints: Trace the existing calculation for a one-cent subtotal with a 50 percent discount.
Python round uses ties-to-even, and bool is a subclass of int. Compare those facts with the disclosed contract.
Use basis-point integer arithmetic: round a nonnegative numerator divided by 10000 by adding 5000 before integer division. Validate each field using an exact integer-type check.

drills.title: Round once and prove it
drills.lesson: Exact integer arithmetic and contract boundaries
drills.exercise: Write a small pure function that discounts 3 cents by 50 percent and explain the result. Add checks distinguishing invoice-level from line-level rounding.

drills.title: Reject integer lookalikes
drills.exercise: Write a validator for nonnegative integer cents. Test True, False, 1.0, "1", None, zero, and a valid large integer; explain why exact type semantics matter.

drills.title: Choose a discriminating money test
drills.exercise: Write three quote checks that distinguish ties-to-even from half-up rounding, line rounding from invoice rounding, and float math from integer math. Explain what each passing check establishes.
